manufacturers.short_history: Ketron is an Italian maker of arranger keyboards, sound modules and digital accordions, working from Ancona since 1981. It started out building electronic organs, then moved the organ production line over to accompaniment instruments when that market collapsed in the middle of the decade. Its breakthrough was the MS series of 1992, the first arrangers designed entirely to its own concept, and it has stayed in that niche ever since, through the X, XD and SD ranges and the audio-based Audya and Event generations.
manufacturers.long_history:
Ketron was set up in February 1981 in Ancona, on Italy's Adriatic coast, to build instruments for solo entertainers and amateurs rather than for studios. Its first product, finished by the end of that year, was a portable organ. In its early years the company worked as an affiliate of the German firm Solton, and a long run of instruments designed and built by the Ancona team went out under the Solton name instead of its own: the Monarch organ, the P600 with its PCM-sampled percussion, the Super Polyvox electronic accordion, and above all the Programmer24 accompaniment unit, which set the pattern the rest of the industry followed.

The company researched digital technology through 1982 and released a digital product in June 1983, keeping that line running until the organ market collapsed in 1985. It survived by turning the organ output into accompaniment instruments and accordion modules, a business that carried it to 1991. That year it went deep into what it called Multisynthesis, and in 1992 launched the MS series. The MS5 and MS4 were the first, followed by the MS50, MS60, MS40 and MS100; the line ran for roughly eight years and made the company known well beyond Italy.

The Solton brand disappeared from Ketron instruments after 2000, the X8 being the last to carry it, and the two companies formally parted in 2003. Ketron consolidated with the X, XD and SD series from 1999 onward, added digital pianos with the DG models from around 2001, and scored a lasting hit with the MidJay module in 2004. In 2008 the Audya series put streamed audio loops into the accompaniment styles for the first time in the arranger sector, replacing synthesised guitar and percussion parts with recordings of real players. The SD line was renewed from 2015, and in 2022 the Event project rebuilt the catalogue around an all-audio arranger. The company remains active in Ancona, and now also sells Solton-branded amplification alongside its own instruments.

sources.value: Ketron began in 1981 as a consociata (affiliate) of the German company Solton; Solton branding ran on Ketron products until 2000 and the two formally separated in 2003
Ketron began in 1981 as a consociata of the German company Solton

manufacturers.review_note: Founders not stated by any source, left empty. The Ketron-Solton relationship is recorded as a collaboration because the Italian sources call Ketron a consociata (affiliate) of Solton but never say which company owned which; ketron.it and the UK distributor do not mention the historical relationship at all. Product-level disagreements, none of which touch a stored manufacturer field: the UK distributor lists the MS series as MS40/MS50-60/MS100 with no MS5 or MS4, while the Italian chronology puts MS5 and MS4 first in 1992 and MS40 only in 1995; the same chronology says the SD renewal happened in 2015 but its own table dates SD40 to 2016 and SD9 to 2017; a reader comment claims audio percussion arrived with the X1 GROOVE, not with Audya in 2008. X8 is filed under Ketron per the chronology table although it was the last model to carry Solton branding. Digital piano years for DG4 and DG5 are not stated. The FS6 pedalboard was left out as an accessory.

Instrument-list-only addition made while researching Ketron 2026-09-03. These models carried the Solton brand but, per a former Ketron employee writing on tastierearranger.com, were designed and built by the Ketron team in Ancona. No year is stated for any of them; the P600 is dated only approximately, around 1984. Project100 and K160 are named in the same source and were already known to us from the sequencer.de index. Polivox and P600C appear only in reader comments and were left out.

manufacturers.short_history: Eminent is a Dutch organ builder that grew out of an organ dealership Jacob Vreeken opened in Bodegraven in 1923. It put its first electronic organ on the market in 1961 and later used Solina as a second brand. Its 310 Unique of 1972 carried a built-in string section, and the standalone version of that section, the Solina String Ensemble, became one of the most widely used keyboards of the seventies. The company survives today in Lelystad, building digital church and home organs.
manufacturers.long_history:
Jacob Vreeken (1899-1976) was a baker's assistant who accompanied the singing at his local church, and in 1923 he decided to start dealing in organs. He financed it by giving organ lessons and overhauling old harmoniums, and he spent half of every guilder of profit on advertising, on the principle that customers who cannot find you cannot buy from you. In 1928 he moved into the centre of Bodegraven and began importing German organs. The trade stopped during the war; in 1945 he briefly planned to switch to selling paintings and abandoned the idea an hour before the shop was due to open, going back to organs instead.

In 1950 he imported the German electronic Multimonica, his first step into electronics, and in 1959 decided to develop an electronic organ of his own. It reached the market in 1961 as the Eminent 60, the first instrument to carry the name. Solina organ production started in 1965, the firm moved to Waddinxveen in 1969 into two factory buildings, and Vreeken stepped down as managing director in 1970 at the age of seventy.

The instrument that made the company known outside the organ world was the Eminent 310 Unique of 1972, the first organ with a string section built in and, by that route, the first commercial polyphonic string synthesiser. The string section was spun out as a standalone keyboard, the Solina String Ensemble of 1974, which ARP Instruments distributed in the United States from 1974 to 1981 as the ARP String Ensemble. It was a Dutch design throughout. Jean-Michel Jarre used the 310 on Oxygene and Equinoxe.

The traditional organ market shrank around 1980. Eminent was close to failure in 1982 and restarted in reduced form; that company went under in 1984 as well, and a new one, Eminent Orgels BV, was set up to sell off the remaining stock and to service and supply parts for existing Eminent and Solina organs. It did well enough to turn to digital organ production from 1990, developing a voicing system in Lelystad that can be adjusted in fine detail to the room an instrument stands in. The firm moved to Lelystad in 1994 and still works from the same building on the Titaanstraat, having thoroughly revised that system in 2012.
manufacturers.review_note: The company's own history page presents an unbroken line from 1923, while nl.wikipedia records two bankruptcies (1982 and 1984) and a new legal entity, Eminent Orgels BV, founded afterwards. Both accounts are in the prose and no second manufacturer record was created. The legal name is given as Eminent Orgels BV by nl.wikipedia and as Eminent Orgelbouw B.V. by en.wikipedia; long_name was left empty rather than pick one. The ARP distribution deal for the Solina String Ensemble (1974-1981, US market) is prose only, not a manufacturer_relations row, because it is distribution rather than ownership. Capella, Amadeus and Positief are current organ lines from the company's own site with no stated year; the E-Serie and CX-Serie labels were left out as range names rather than models.

manufacturers.short_history: Synton was a Dutch maker and importer of electronic music equipment, founded by Felix Visser in 1973. It is remembered for the Syntovox vocoders, for modular systems often built to order for conservatories and music schools, and for the Syrinx, the only keyboard instrument it ever made. The company went bankrupt in 1989, but two of its people revived the name in 1997 with the Fenix modular, which ran in small batches into the 2010s.
manufacturers.long_history:
Felix Visser started Synton in the Netherlands in 1973. Alongside its own production the company was the main European importer for E-mu, Ensoniq and Fairlight, which put it at the centre of the Dutch electronic music scene of the period. Its own instruments went in two directions. The Syntovox vocoders, models 202, 216, 221 and 222, were the products that carried the name furthest. The modular systems, sold as the System 300, System 700 and System 3000, were frequently tailored to the requirements of individual conservatories and music schools rather than sold as a fixed catalogue product. Around those sat a range of studio modules and effects: phasers, flangers, a Time Machine, voltage-controlled filters, equalisers, crossovers and mixer series, which are not counted here as instruments.

Synton built exactly one keyboard instrument, the monophonic Syrinx of 1983-1984, designed by Bert Vermeulen. Marc Paping worked as the company's product specialist. The company went bankrupt in 1989.

In 1997 Paping and Vermeulen brought the name back for the Fenix, an analogue modular system of 31 modules, of which around 75 were built between 1997 and 2000. A second run followed in 2010 with 75 units of the Fenix II and 25 of the sequencer-equipped Fenix III, and the line later extended to the Fenix IID and Fenix IV. Separately, Visser worked with Vermeulen on Syntonovo, a five-dimensional touch-sensitive keyboard shown as three prototypes at Superbooth in 2017, 2018 and 2019. Felix Visser died on 17 December 2025.
manufacturers.review_note: Status defunct rests on a single non-official source, en.wikipedia's Synton Fenix article; dutchsynth.eu writes about the company only in the past tense, which is not a stated fact. synton.nl is named by dutchsynth.eu as the place where Synton information is published, but the host refuses TLS and redirects to dutchsynth.eu, so it was not usable as an official source and official_website was left empty. Founding city not stated; dutchsynth.eu's strapline says the instruments were designed in Traiectum, the Latin name for Utrecht, which is a hint rather than a statement, so city was left empty. Model-list disagreement: en.wikipedia names a System 2000 and System 3000, while dutchsynth.eu has System 300, System 700 and System 3000; all four are recorded and none is dropped. The Syntovox vocoders are recorded as instruments; if vocoders should be treated as processors rather than instruments, these four rows are the ones to revisit. The company's phasers, flangers, Time Machine, filters, equalisers, crossovers and mixer series were left out as effects, per the scope rule. Syntonovo, the five-dimensional keyboard collaboration between Felix Visser, Bert Vermeulen and Thinrs, produced three prototypes shown at Superbooth 2017-2019; it is described as a collaboration rather than a company and got no record of its own.

manufacturers.short_history: Studio Electronics is an American maker of discrete analogue synthesizers. It began by rackmounting and retrofitting other companies' instruments, among them the Minimoog, the Prophet-5 and the Oberheim OB-8, and only later built its own from scratch, starting with the Midimini. The SE-1, ATC-1 and Omega 8 established it in the nineties and two-thousands, the Boomstar range extended it to desktop and eurorack formats, and in 2017 it co-developed the SE-02 with Roland.
manufacturers.long_history:
Studio Electronics started as a business that took existing analogue synthesizers and rebuilt them into rackmount, MIDI-controllable form. Minimoogs, Sequential Circuits Prophet-5s and Oberheim OB-8s all went through that treatment, which is where the company learned the discrete analogue circuitry it has stayed with since. Its own site places the start of that work in 1985 and describes it as the kitchen table days; English Wikipedia dates the company to 1981.

The Midimoog of 1989 still followed the retrofit pattern. The Midimini was the first instrument the company designed from scratch rather than converting, and the firm still treats it as the pivot in its own story. The SE-1 followed in 1993 and became the product the company is best known for, a monophonic rackmount whose bass and lead sounds turned up across nineties dance and electronic records; it was revised as the SE-1X in 2000. Alongside it the ATC-1 of 1996, the Analog Tone Chameleon, took interchangeable filter cartridges so that one instrument could be given the character of a Minimoog, a TB-303, an ARP 2600 or an Oberheim SEM. The ATC-X followed in 2003, and the eight-voice, multitimbral Omega 8 and the Modmax series arrived in 2004.

The Boomstar series from 2014 moved the same discrete circuitry into desktop boxes and, as Boomstar Modular, into eurorack, joined by the Quadnic and the Tonestar 2600 in 2016. In 2017 the company worked with Roland on the SE-02, a three-oscillator analogue synthesizer sold under the Roland name. The current line runs to the CODE and CODE Luxe polyphonics, the paraphonic SE-3X, a thirtieth-anniversary Midimini V30, the Omega 8 and the SE-1X, with the Red Eye, ATC-Xi and Orion listed as legacy instruments.
conflicts: founding year: 1985 per the company's own site (studioelectronics.com/products/synths/boomstar/, twice: "where STUDIO ELECTRONICS started in 1985") vs 1981 per en.wikipedia. The two sources describe the same event, the start of the company, so this is not an operational-versus-legal date split. The official value was written into the column per the tier order.
manufacturers.review_note: Country rests on a single non-official source; the company's own pages never state where it is based, and repeated attempts at an About, History, Company or Contact page returned 404 or 403. Founding city therefore left empty, although secondary references place the company in the Los Angeles area. Founders not stated anywhere: Marc St. Regis and Greg St. Regis appear throughout the company's own news pages as the people running it, but no source calls them founders, so the field was left empty. The Roland SE-02 (2017) was deliberately NOT added as a Studio Electronics instrument: it was co-developed but sold under Roland's name, which fails the own-name test. The EXT Box was left out as a controller and the software editors as software.

manufacturers.short_history: JoMoX is a Berlin maker of analogue drum machines and synthesizers, run by Juergen Michaelis. The name came out of a logo he drew as J*M*X, for Juergen Michaelis X-Tended, whose asterisks read as Os. Its first product, the XBase 09 of 1996, was an analogue answer to the Roland TR-909 and is still the instrument the company is asked for most; the line runs from there through the XBase 888 and 999 to the SunSyn polysynth and the current Alpha Base.
manufacturers.long_history:
JoMoX began with small MIDI interfaces built by Juergen Michaelis. In 1995, working in the technicians' collective X-Tended, he drew a logo reading J*M*X, short for Juergen Michaelis X-Tended; the asterisks between the letters looked like the letter O, and the name JoMoX stuck. English Wikipedia dates the company itself to 1997.

The first product was the XBase 09 in 1996, an analogue drum machine built around the sounds of the Roland TR-909 at a time when the originals were becoming expensive. It has stayed the company's signature instrument. The AirBase99 followed in 1998, and in 2000 the company moved well beyond drums with the SunSyn, an eight-voice analogue polysynth. The Resonator Neuronium of 2002 was stranger still, an experimental analogue instrument built on a neural network principle. The JaZBase03 and the MBase01 kick drum module arrived in 2003, the XBase 999 in 2006 and the XBase 888 in 2008, alongside a run of filter and resonator units.

From 2009 the catalogue moved towards single-voice percussion modules and eurorack: the MBase 11 in 2009, the M.Brane 11 in 2010 with the SunSyn Mk2, then the ModBase09 and Mod.Brane11 in 2013. The Alpha Base of 2016, an eleven-part analogue drum machine with sample and FM channels, is the current flagship and has since been revised as the Alpha Base mk II. The company still operates from Berlin.
manufacturers.review_note: The company's own Company page dates the J*M*X logo and the first MIDI interfaces to 1995 but never states a founding year; the 1997 in the column comes from en.wikipedia. These are plausibly two different events, the start of the work and the founding of the GmbH, so it was not recorded as a conflict. Product years come from the company's own dated list, which is explicitly described there as incomplete. The filter and effect units on that list, T-Resonator, T-Resonator Mk2, M-Resonator, T-Rackonizer and MoonWind, were left out of the instruments table under the scope rule, as were the MIDI-to-CV interfaces. Berlin as the city rests on a single source.

manufacturers.short_history: Quasimidi was a German maker of synthesizers and grooveboxes, founded in Kirchhain in 1987 by Friedhelm Haar and Joerg Reichstein. It started with MIDI processors and master keyboards, then built its reputation on instruments aimed squarely at nineties dance music: the Quasar, the Technox, and above all the Rave-O-Lution 309, which took on Roland in the groovebox market. It was among the makers that put knobs and sliders back on the front panel. The company left the market in 2000 and went into insolvency in 2001.
manufacturers.long_history:
Quasimidi was founded in 1987 in Kirchhain, in Hesse, by Friedhelm Haar and Joerg Reichstein, and moved to nearby Rauschenberg in 1998. Its first work was on the MIDI market rather than in sound generation: a Merge-Monster merge box, the Turbo Volcon/D master keyboard controller, and the Style Drive MIDI processor with its Style-Drive-Commander remote, which drove accompaniment styles from a sequencer.

The move into instruments came with the Quasar in 1994, a rack synthesizer that could be extended with the TRE and RAM modules and later the Hardcore expansion, whose sound sets were pitched directly at techno and dance producers. The Raven and the Cyber-6 of 1995 were performance keyboards built on the same engine, and the Technox of the same year put it in a rack. The Rave-O-Lution 309 of 1996 was the instrument that made the company's name: a standalone groovebox with analogue-modelled bass and drum sounds, an onboard sequencer and part muting for live use, released into the same market Roland was addressing with the MC-303. The Sirius of 1997 extended the idea to a keyboard with a hybrid engine the company called DTE, Digital True Emulation, with a vocoder, drums and multitimbral sequencing on board. The Polymorph rack synthesizer of 1999 was the last major product.

Quasimidi was gone from the market by 2000 and went into insolvency in 2001. Its instruments have kept a following since, and the 309 and the Sirius in particular are still sought after.
manufacturers.review_note: Two end dates that are two different events, not a contradiction: de.wikipedia says the company had not been present on the market since 2000 and went into insolvency in 2001, en.wikipedia says it folded in 2000. ended_year holds the legal date, 2001, and the prose keeps both. Product years differ between sources and are recorded here as detail rather than as manufacturer-level conflicts: Quasar 1993 (de) vs 1994 (en and the legacy site); Turbo Volcon/D 1989 (de) vs 1991 (legacy site); Raven 1995 (de, en) vs 1996 (legacy site); Rave-O-Lution 309 1996 (en) vs 1997 (legacy site); Sirius 1997 (de, en) vs 1998 (legacy site); Polymorph 1998 (de) vs 1999 (en and legacy site). Where two sources agreed, that year was taken. Left out of the instruments table: the Merge-Monster MIDI merge box and the Style Drive MIDI processor with its Style-Drive-Commander remote, as neither generates sound, and the TRE, RAM and Hardcore expansion boards, as they are options for the Quasar rather than instruments. The master keyboards Turbo Volcon/D, Raven and Cyber-6 were kept, since MIDI keyboards count as instruments under the scope rule. The company's site, quasimidi.eu, exists only in the Web Archive, so official_website was left empty.

manufacturers.short_history: Multivox was an American brand of synthesizers, string machines and drum machines, sold out of New York from the mid-1940s as the manufacturing arm of the Peter Sorkin Music Company and best known for its instruments of the late seventies. Almost none of them were designed or built in the United States: the electronics came from the small Japanese maker Hillwood, which also sold under its own Firstman name, so a Multivox and its Japanese or European sibling were frequently the same instrument with a different badge. The brand disappeared in the early eighties.
manufacturers.long_history:
Multivox was founded in the mid-1940s in New York as the guitar and amplifier manufacturing subsidiary of the Peter Sorkin Music Company, and for its first decades that was its business, along with the Premier brand of guitars, amplifiers, PA and hi-fi gear it shared with its parent. The Premier Model 90 reverb unit of the early sixties competed with Fender's, and Premier amplifiers are still sought by blues harmonica players.

The synthesizer years came later and were run on a different model. From 1976 Multivox had its instruments built in Japan by Hillwood, a small manufacturer founded in 1972 by Kazuo Morioka, which sold the same designs at home under the Firstman name. The arrangement ran to about 1980. The consequence is visible inside the instruments: the Multivox MX202 string and brass machine of 1977 and Roland's RS202 of 1976 are the same instrument at board level, because Hillwood built both. The catalogue that resulted was wide and cheap, running from the small MX-20 and MX-30 monosynths through the MX-880 and MX-2000 duophonics to the MX-3000, along with the MX-150 Basky bass synth, the MX-57 Electro-Snare and, in 1981, the SQ-01, a sequencer with a small synthesizer built in that had been released in Japan a year earlier as a Firstman.

The company was contemporary with, and often unfavourably compared to, Roland; its reputation has improved since, largely because the Japanese origins of the designs became better understood. Sorkin Music closed in the mid-1970s and Multivox continued for roughly fourteen years afterwards, disappearing in the early 1980s. Its later address was Hauppauge, New York.

sources.value: Multivox had its instruments built by Hillwood of Japan from 1976 to 1980; Hillwood also traded as Firstman
Firstman, also known as Hillwood, founded 1972 by Kazuo Morioka; the SQ-01 came out under Firstman in 1980 before Multivox released it in 1981

manufacturers.review_note: Status defunct is stated by en.wikipedia alone, which is why this record lands on needs_review; no second source says in so many words that the company ended, they only write about it in the past tense. founded_year and ended_year were left empty on purpose: the sources say mid-1940s and early 1980s, which are not years. Founders not stated. IMPORTANT for the queue: Hillwood (queue row 620) and Firstman (queue row 484) are the same Japanese company, founded 1972 by Kazuo Morioka, per electronicmusic.fandom.com; the relation here creates a Hillwood stub, so those two queue rows should be merged before Firstman is researched separately. The Peter Sorkin Music Company deliberately got no record of its own, under the holding-company rule; its role is in the prose. Left out of the instruments table: the Big Jam SE-1 to SE-18 guitar pedals as effects, and the Rhythm Ace FR-3S and FR6M, which are Ace Tone products and whose appearance in the Multivox sources could not be verified as a rebadge.
